residue.text: Retained unresolved mechanism: agitation-generated disturbance and the optical-to-agitation return loop are hypotheses; specks do not identify bubbles. Matched 900 rpm final samples and isolated bubble measurements are absent. Proposed alternative allocation: compare timer-stopped 60-second 900 rpm with enabled optical control capped at second 105, logging shadow decisions and sampling both at second 120. Hypothesis: both pass while timer control reduces stirring; rival prediction: only longer stirring passes. Neither result proves the specific speed or rule necessary.

Retained proposed reversed-arrow test, omitted from the six-repeat construction: compare fixed 300/900 rpm 60-second runs and images after cessation. Hypothesis: agitation produces transient optical spread despite successful final samples. Persistent spread or sample failure could favor gradients or persistent artifacts. Optional reverse-order repeats pause at seconds 45-50 and stop at second 65, preserving 60 stirring seconds. This requires reallocating trials within the six-trial limit; pauses change settling and transport, so rapid image changes cannot identify bubbles or establish prior uniformity.

Retained limits: relative 900 rpm sample performance and actual time savings remain undetermined. Enabled and timer-stopped comparisons can have unequal quiet durations; record cessation times. Commanded speed lacks independent verification. Sampling and transfers can disturb gradients; order dependence weakens inference. Common-aliquot repeatability is not concentration calibration. Six trials constrain replication and causal strength.

Source-bound omitted option: syringe withdrawal low and return high permits bulk redistribution or combination with rotation; no successful transfer construction is observed. Any proposed benefit is a hypothesis, and transfers may disturb gradients. Other viscosities, solutes, vessel sizes and continuous processes remain untested; claims stay within this synthetic sample proxy, with no real chemical or human benefit established.

summary.text: Retain the main hypothesis: fixed 300 rpm for 60 seconds can repeatedly satisfy the final depth-sample target without optical control. Observed attenuations 0.204, 0.209 and 0.207 give approximately 2.4 percent spread in one trial, opposing universal necessity of sustained 900 rpm. Repeat success is unobserved. Rival hypothesis: this success was exceptional or sampling-mediated; repeated failure or sampling-order dependence would weaken reliable sufficiency without proving 900 rpm necessary.

Proposed construction: six fresh, rinsed-vessel trials within 90 minutes, each using 150 mL water and 0.30 mL dye, one bottle, locked camera and fixed addition location. Command 300 rpm for exactly 60 seconds; stop regardless of optical spread and do not restart before second-120 sampling. Use the spill tray and stop if liquid escapes.

Log five-second side readings, frames, depression, specks, commanded speed, timing and transfers. At second 120, withdraw 1 mL from each marked depth within ten seconds; alternate sampling order. Use water and common-aliquot references. Report raw attenuations, normalized spread, duration and every failure above 4 percent. Hypothesized repeated success requires final samples; stable side images alone cannot establish it.
